title: 'Waste of energy': Senate Democrats are sitting out the John Fetterman pile-on
description: The unpredictable Pennsylvania senator is absorbing a massive intraparty backlash. But not from his Senate colleagues.
fullText:
Sen. John Fetterman has faced a tide of public criticism from fellow Democrats as he stakes out lonely ground as a critic of the far-left wing of his party — and another wave rolled in Wednesday after he made a surprise video appearance at the Republican midterm convention.

So far, however, his Senate colleagues haven't joined the pile-on.

Democratic senators are staying above the fray as they work to flip the majority in November amid constant speculation that the 57-year-old Pennsylvanian could trigger a nightmare scenario by leaving the party and caucusing with the GOP.

Some have worked to publicly bat down suggestions that Fetterman could abandon Democrats for the final two years of his term — something he has denied considering, even as he continues to raise eyebrows with his outspoken support of Israel, bashing of democratic socialists and close relationships with Senate Republicans.

"John Fetterman is a friend and an important member of our caucus. It's a waste of energy to get spun up about his voting record or place in our party — he votes with us 90 percent of the time," Democratic Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont, who is close with Fetterman, said in a statement to POLITICO before the convention appearance. "We need a big tent if we're going to win in November."

That silence could be tested in the coming weeks. Recent reports, including in The Wall Street Journal, detailed how he has skipped meetings with key constituencies and largely stopped participating in caucus lunches or committee meetings. Fetterman denounced the report as "lies, half-truths, innuendos, [and] smears" peddled by "disgruntled staffers."

A social media account purported to be run by former Fetterman aides has teased the release next week of additional stories and evidence related to his job performance, which could spark a new wave of questions for the senator and his colleagues once they return Monday from a five-week summer recess.

Fetterman further fueled party-switch chatter with a recent appearance with Pennsylvania's Republican senator, David McCormick — then heaping praise on McCormick in the convention video Wednesday, where he also pledged to "work with" President Donald Trump to protect his state's steel industry.

In a statement Wednesday, Fetterman said his Republican convention remarks were intended to pay tribute to McCormick "as a great American and friend."

"We are in different parties, but we are both Team PA," he said. "We have delivered hundreds of millions of dollars back to Pennsylvania, fought for improved transportation and affordable housing, and the Steel Way of Life."

"I'm a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party — and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on," he added.

If any Democrats fear driving Fetterman into the GOP's arms with intraparty criticism, some of his potential 2028 competitors aren't among them.

Former Rep. Conor Lamb, who lost to Fetterman in 2022 and is mulling a 2028 bid, said in an interview that he's believed for close to a year that his onetime Democratic primary foe would become a Republican — a position he acknowledged puts him "in the minority."

"I don't think anything I say, or anyone who is a Democrat says, affects him all that much," Lamb said, adding, "The fact that the Senate Democratic leadership thinks they can keep them on their team by saying a few nice things about him in public just shows that they haven't learned who they are dealing with."

Pennsylvania Rep. Chris Deluzio, a Democrat who is also mulling a 2028 Senate bid, also shrugged off a question about if the public criticism of Fetterman — who he accused of "undermining our efforts to take back the House" — could drive the senator to become a Republican.

"In the two years he has left in this job, in this term, he should be a Democrat," Deluzio said. "That is what the people of Pennsylvania elected him to do. That is what they expect him to do, that is what I would say he should do with what he has left in the Senate."

Still, Senate Democrats have largely avoided casting aspersions. Republicans hold a three-seat advantage, and Democrats believe they are in striking distance of picking up the four seats they'd need to win control. A post-election Fetterman flip could put the Senate back to 50-50, giving Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote.

Multiple Democratic senators approached by POLITICO this week about Fetterman simply declined to comment. Asked in a late July news conference if he wanted Fetterman to stay in the party, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he did.

"He is a very good member of Congress," he said. "The people in our caucus very much like him and respect him, and we're a big tent party. We can have a lot of different views in that party."

A Senate Democratic aide — who, like others quoted for this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly — said Democrats "are keen on batting down" the speculation that Fetterman would split from the caucus.

Fetterman has repeatedly downplayed that possibility. In May he wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he had "no plans to leave" the Democratic Party and that he would be a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." In July, at the Hill Nation summit, he appeared to anticipate being a pivotal member of the party next year.

"If I was going to, I would have already done that," Fetterman said in July about a party switch. "And I would remind everybody, we are talking about how it's possible, how we could retain the majority in the Senate — well, that's because I make that mathematically possible. And if we flip those four seats, then I would be 51."

But he laid out a red line, saying there was "one condition" where he would abandon the Democrats — if they become "the anti-Israel party."

Privately, many Senate Democratic colleagues profess to be in the dark about what Fetterman is thinking. Though his colleagues are collegial, he frequently sits alone off the Senate floor during votes.

"I really don't have any insight into that," said one Senate Democrat when asked about the party-switch chatter.

There's been speculation within the Senate for months that Fetterman would simply retire rather than mount a difficult reelection campaign in 2028, driven by the widespread view that he doesn't enjoy the job. Fetterman has sidestepped questions about a second term, arguing that it is too early for such questions.

A second Senate Democratic aide added that there was "definitely a concern" about Fetterman but that he still voted "pretty solidly" with Democrats.

"There's a hope that a lot of this is just positioning … and not a real possibility," the aide said. "Hopefully they can find a way to keep him in the fold, but it's not really clear what he actually wants."

A third Senate Democratic aide acknowledged the internal rumors about what he would do while adding that Fetterman and his office are "insular" — making it difficult for anyone outside of his inner circle to know what he's thinking. A fourth added that Senate Democrats weren't taking the speculation that Fetterman could flip "too seriously" for now.

But the aide added that Fetterman could make the caucus' life "harder if he ends up being the 51st vote if the majority is in hand next January."

Republicans, meanwhile, have made it clear that they are trying to recruit Fetterman. McCormick publicly defended him amid the latest round of Democratic backlash, and Majority Leader John Thune told reporters recently that he and other Republican senators have had "conversations" with Fetterman and "would welcome the opportunity" to have him join the GOP.

Only 22% of self-identified Democratic voters in a recent New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll have a favorable opinion of Fetterman, compared to 73% of self-identified Republicans.

But it's far from clear that Fetterman could win a GOP primary given that he still votes with Democrats most of the time.

Lamb said Fetterman's inability to prevail in a Democratic primary in 2028 was "as sure a fact as gravity" and added that the senator's path in a GOP primary wouldn't be easy, either.

"I think there are probably people in the state who would run against him if he was in a Republican primary," Lamb said.

Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) said that he takes Fetterman "at his word" that he's a Democrat and said he doubted he'd ever be fully embraced by GOP primary voters. He cited Fetterman's poor ratings from key groups influential on the right, such as the National Rifle Association and National Federation of Independent Business.

"He's a good man. Like I said, he's got courage," he said, before adding, "He's a Democrat and maybe a traditional Democrat, so I don't think that would be something the Republican Party would embrace."

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

title: Wall Street has thrown in the towel on a quick end to the global oil shock
description: Oil analysts are raising 2027 forecasts as disrupted Middle East shipping, shrinking stockpiles, and inflation risks linger.
fullText:
Wall Street is raising its 2027 oil forecasts with a quick return to normal looking less and less likely.

The longer crude stays elevated, the more pressure builds on consumers, inflation, bonds, and stocks.

Around the time Ben Shelton was polishing off his US Open victory over Carlos Alcaraz in the wee hours of Wednesday morning, the price of oil was making some waves of its own, climbing back above $100 per barrel.

The break into triple digits was weeks in the making. After falling below $80 in early August, oil has been on a mostly uninterrupted climb higher. Any optimism traders have around an Iran-war resolution has fizzled. They're now (re)pricing for a prolonged disruption.

But while $100 is an important psychological milestone, a deeper shift is occurring across Wall Street. There's a growing recognition that the global oil shock may not fade as quickly as investors once hoped.

Perhaps the most drastic reaction to oil's latest spike came from HSBC, which lifted its 2027 Brent forecast by a whopping $20, to $85. The firm's base case is that Strait of Hormuz flows will recover only gradually, continuing the ongoing supply squeeze.

Then there's Goldman Sachs, which raised its 2027 forecast to $80, while also flagging a worst-case scenario of $120 oil where Gulf output remains suppressed.

Not to be outdone, Bank of America said continued Middle East conflict could put oil in a $95-to-$120 range, with $150 a possibility if energy infrastructure is damaged further.

Even if those forecasts remain below oil's current price, Wall Street is now treating triple-digit crude as a realistic outcome rather than a remote risk.

Three forces are combining to sustain the ongoing oil shock. First, the Strait of Hormuz — despite occasional signs of progress — is still operating well below normal capacity.

Second, the oil stockpiles being used to cushion the blow to prices are getting thinner with every delayed shipment.

And finally, while workarounds and new routes have offered relief, they haven't helped enough to avoid a full-blown supply crisis. The old normal is far from being restored, and may never be.

A prolonged stretch of $100-plus crude oil impacts consumers well beyond the gas pump (although that certainly hurts too). It also means higher prices for diesel, jet fuel, and shipping, which can eventually touch nearly everything people spend money on: groceries, deliveries, flights, and utilities, just to name a few.

title: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia’s Arctic gas heartland as Trump pushes Putin toward peace
description: Ukrainian drones struck Novy Urengoy, sparking a fire in Russia's top natural-gas region roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border in the Arctic.
fullText:
Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia's Arctic north Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia's most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and the Associated Press.

Regional Gov. Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site. He did not identify the facility, and the extent of the damage was still being assessed, Reuters reported Wednesday.

Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting: "Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target."

The extraordinary strike comes as Washington makes a renewed push to end the more than four-year war even as Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on each other.

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had just spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both Moscow and Kyiv may be prepared to negotiate.

"We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice," Trump said.

Asked what was holding up an agreement, Trump pointed to the personal animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling them "two people that hate each other."

"These are two people that are tired of fighting," Trump added.

Trump's comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive negotiations. The talks produced no breakthrough, according to the Associated Press.

Russian Strikes Continue Following Visit By Witkoff And Kushner To Kyiv

Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left Ukraine, killing five people and wounding 35 on Tuesday, Reuters reported.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a long-standing dilemma for Western governments trying to engage Moscow.

"You have to talk, you have to explain," the source said, arguing that communication is necessary to prevent misunderstandings.

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

But the source said Russian officials can interpret Western outreach differently.

"Whenever you talk with them, they consider that this is a Western weakness," the source said, adding that the assessment was based in part on informal contacts with Russian officials.

The source also said Putin's recent emphasis on Russian "military progress in Ukraine" appeared aimed in part at Washington, projecting strength as U.S. officials seek to revive negotiations.

The escalation is taking an increasing toll on civilians. The United Nations said last month that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded.

More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its strikes are aimed at military and military-related facilities.

Drone Offensive Hits Russian Oil Tankers And Refineries At 'Industrial Scale' As Moscow Bans Diesel Exports

United24 described Wednesday's attack as the deepest Ukrainian drone strike inside Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Novy Urengoy lies roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border. Artem Zhoga, Putin's envoy to Russia's Urals Federal District, said a Ukrainian drone had attempted to strike a fuel-and-energy facility in Yamal, according to Meduza.

The city sits in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, the country's dominant natural-gas producing region. About 80% of Russia's natural gas is extracted there, according to Interfax data cited by the Associated Press.

Artyukhov said there were no reported casualties.

The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault on Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck targets around the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, including a naval base, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships capable of carrying cruise missiles, according to the Associated Press.

Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in the Novorossiysk attack.

Russia, meanwhile, continued its own long-range campaign against Ukraine Wednesday. Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while another wave of attacks on Kyiv killed one person and wounded 14, according to Reuters.
